title: Quantum-information fingerprints of partial dynamical symmetry in the interacting boson model
abstract: Partial dynamical symmetry (PDS) is an algebraic structure in which a prescribed symmetry is neither exact nor completely broken: a subset of eigenstates keeps good quantum numbers and remains solvable while the rest of the spectrum mixes. PDS is currently identified from spectroscopic data, band-head energies, level systematics, and $B(E2)$ ratios. We ask whether it also has a purely structural signature in the eigenstates, and find that it does, though not in the magnitude of entanglement. The natural diagnostic is the variance of a symmetry Casimir, the label variance $\Var\,\C[G]$, which we show coincides with a block-coherence entropy and a block impurity: all three vanish exactly when a state carries a single irreducible-representation label. Resolved state by state, this quantity is zero on the solvable subset and of order $N^2$ on the mixed states, at stable symmetry points and at Leviatan's first- and second-order critical points, where it takes two distinct forms set by the order of the transition. The magnitude of bipartite entanglement, by contrast, does not separate solvable from mixed states and drifts even where the labels are exact. We anchor the analysis in $^{168}$Er, connect the block purity to the ``purity/coherence'' language of the quasi-dynamical-symmetry literature, and show the label variance is uncorrelated with multipartite entanglement and with magic. Finally we encode the model on a qubit register and prepare its solvable and mixed eigenstates variationally, as a step toward evaluating the diagnostic on a quantum device.
summary: This work introduces the 'label variance' ($	ext{Var}\,\C[G]$) as a novel and robust quantum information diagnostic to detect Partial Dynamical Symmetry (PDS) in the Interacting Boson Model. It demonstrates that this structural measure successfully distinguishes between solvable and mixed eigenstates, unlike standard entanglement measures. The authors validate this method by encoding the model onto qubits, paving the way for its direct evaluation on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is determining if Partial Dynamical Symmetry (PDS) possesses a purely structural signature within quantum eigenstates, independent of entanglement magnitude.
main_result: The label variance ($	ext{Var}\,\C[G]$) serves as this robust, fit-independent diagnostic, successfully separating solvable states (zero variance) from mixed states ($\mathcal{O}(N^2)$).
method: The authors compare structural diagnostics like label variance against entanglement measures and test the method's feasibility by encoding the Hamiltonian onto a qubit register for variational state preparation.
model_or_system: The analysis is based on the Interacting Boson Model (IBM) applied to even-even nuclei, specifically anchored in $^{168}	ext{Er}$. The model Hamiltonian supports various symmetry limits, including those exhibiting PDS.
key_observables: Label variance ($	ext{Var}\,\C[G]$), block-coherence entropy ($S_G$), and block impurity ($P_G$).
important_parameters: The total boson number $N$, and the Hamiltonian parameters defining critical points (e.g., $ eta_0$ for first/second order transitions).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the label variance correctly captures the structural distinction between solvable and mixed spectral subsets, even when entanglement measures fail to do so.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how label variance distinguishes solvable (rigid) from mixed states, and later show the successful application of VQE/VQD protocols on a qubit register to prepare these distinct eigenstates.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical equivalence between vanishing variance, zero entropy, and unit purity for PDS. It then compares this structural diagnostic against entanglement measures using the IBM spectrum. Finally, it details the implementation by encoding the model onto qubits and preparing states variationally on a quantum device.
why_interesting: The development of label variance as a measurable, structure-revealing quantum invariant provides a powerful tool for classifying complex many-body systems whose symmetries are only partially preserved in nature or theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Decision gate at a stable SU(3)-PDS point (N = 10). The static magnitude of the s|d entanglement entropy does not separate solvable (exact-label) from mixed eigenstates: the distributions overlap, and within a fixed angular momentum the solvable states are in fact more entangled (a Simpson’s-paradox reversal). Entanglement magnitude alone is therefore not a PDS diagnostic.

Figure 2: Cone rigidity at a stable SU(3)-PDS point (N = 10). The off-diagonal coupling RD = ∥Q D|ψ⟩∥measures the first-order response of each eigenstate to a deformation along direction D. Along the PDS-preserving directions h0 and h4 every solvable state is rigid to numerical zero (R ≲3 × 10−10, lower band) while every mixed state responds strongly (R ≳70, upper band); the separation is direction-selective, since along the SU(3)-breaking direction ˆnd the solvable states respond as much as the mixed ones (R ∼1, right). Rigidity is a property of the PDS-preserving operator cone, not of the states in isolation.

Figure 4: Second-order critical point, Eq. (6), N = 10 (type II). Every eigenstate carries an exact O(5) seniority: maxψ Var ˆC2[O(5)] = 2.7 × 10−11 over the whole spectrum (left). The s|d entanglement is graded monotonically by τ (right), ⟨S⟩= 0.71 at τ = 0 falling to 0.00 at τ = N: the entanglement lives in the low-seniority sector and high-seniority states are near-product. This seniority-graded ladder differs qualitatively from the first-order solvable-subset picture of Fig. 3.

Figure 5: The purity/coherence bridge on Kremer et al.’s own states, N = 12. The O(6) block purity Trρ2 σ (left) and the bipartite s|d entanglement entropy (centre) are independent axes: the ground state becomes O(6)-pure (Trρ2 σ = 0.81–0.88) precisely where its s|d entanglement is maximal (right). The algebraic “purity” of the quasi-dynamical-symmetry literature and bipartite entanglement are logically independent QI quantities. Our O(6) machinery reproduces Kremer’s σ-fluctuation ∆σgs = 2.473 at the U(5) limit (their value 2.47) and the exactly sharp O(6) point.
